name: vip
desc: Program that provides for interactive editing in a pipeline
why: An old Duke pipeline editor that lets you interactively rework streams, a relic of a different style of computing.

brief.what_it_is: vip is a command-line program, distributed as a Bourne shell script, for interactively editing a data pipeline. The homepage says it 'can be used syntactically like a filter,' so it sits in a shell pipe and takes the stream passing through it. The homepage does not say what it emits or exactly how the interactive editing is done. A ;login: magazine article from October 1997 ('Toolman Edits Pipes -- Interactively!') is linked as the main description, but the plain-text and HTML copies I tried to reach were not available.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage gives no problem statement beyond the one-line description. The only framing offered is the 1997 ;login: article title, 'Toolman Edits Pipes -- Interactively!'.
brief.install_notes: The homepage offers the program as a Bourne shell script of about 3 KB, plus a troff man page (vip.man) and PostScript man page. No install steps, dependencies, or configuration are given on the homepage. The Homebrew metadata lists a 'vip' executable.
brief.standout: It is a small shell-script tool from 1997 that lets you edit a pipeline's contents while it runs, rather than rewriting the pipeline and rerunning it. The author treats this as the point of the tool, and it is described with the phrase 'Toolman Edits Pipes.'
brief.status: quiet. The homepage says 'Last update: 12/17/97' and the author, Daniel E. Singer of Duke's Computer Science department, is named as the maintainer with an email contact. I found no repository, release list, or newer activity, so I can't tell whether it is abandoned or just unchanged.
brief.caveats: Very thin documentation on the homepage. The man page and article links I tried returned 404 at the paths I guessed from the file list, so the actual usage and options are unverified. Platform support, license, and whether it still runs on current shells are not stated. The page is dated 1997.

entry.title: vip
entry.tldr: A 1997 Bourne shell script that drops into the middle of a pipe so you can edit the stream by hand before it moves on.
entry.deeper_look:
vip is a small shell script, about 3 KB, that "provides for interactive editing in a pipeline." The homepage says it "can be used syntactically like a filter," so it goes between two commands in a pipe and takes whatever flows through it.

The idea underneath is a different way of building pipelines. Normally you write a pipeline, run it, look at the output, tweak a stage, and run it all again. vip puts a human in the middle of the stream. The author's 1997 ;login: article is titled "Toolman Edits Pipes -- Interactively!", and that title is about the only framing the homepage offers.

The homepage does not say what editor vip opens, what it emits, or what options it takes. The man page and article links did not load when checked, so the details are unverified. Treat it as a small, old artifact to read: a short shell script is easy to open and see how it works. It was written by Daniel E. Singer at Duke Computer Science, and the page was last updated 12/17/97.

try_this.what_happens: Asks the script for usage. The homepage documents no options, so what this prints is unverified.

entry.whats_unique: Most pipeline tools transform a stream automatically. vip is a filter that stops the stream so a person can edit it before it continues.
entry.caveats: Documentation is thin, the man page and article were unreachable, and the page has not been updated since 1997, so behavior on current shells is unverified.
